scenes.tts: In a newborn mouse brain, some connections will be lost. Which ones, and what carries them away?
scenes.visual: Title card: Which Inputs Lose? A coronal outline of a newborn mouse brain.
scenes.narration: In a newborn mouse brain, some connections will be lost. Which ones, and what carries them away?

scenes.tts: Start in the visual thalamus, the relay where axons from the eye end.
scenes.visual: Zoom to one dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus; label: dLGN, the visual relay in the thalamus. Retinal axons arrive from the optic tract.
scenes.narration: Start in the visual thalamus, the relay where axons from the eye end.

scenes.tts: In a newborn mouse, inputs from the two eyes overlap there.
scenes.visual: Red axons (one eye) and blue axons (the other eye) fill the same region, mixing to purple. Label: newborn.
scenes.narration: In a newborn mouse, inputs from the two eyes overlap there.

scenes.tts: Over roughly the first week and a half, the two eyes' inputs sort into separate territories.
scenes.visual: The red and blue fields pull apart. On-screen clock: about P3 to P10 (postnatal days 3 to 10).
scenes.narration: Over roughly the first week and a half, the two eyes' inputs sort into separate territories.

scenes.tts: Each side ends up mostly the territory of the opposite eye. The eye on the same side keeps a small patch.
scenes.visual: Final map: a large field for the opposite eye and a small patch for the same-side eye. Labels: opposite eye; same-side eye. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Each side ends up mostly the territory of the opposite eye. The eye on the same side keeps a small patch.

scenes.tts: One relay neuron starts with many retinal inputs, and ends with only a few.
scenes.visual: One relay neuron with about ten retinal axons converging; over time most fade, leaving one or two. Label: schematic, not counts.
scenes.narration: One relay neuron starts with many retinal inputs, and ends with only a few.

scenes.visual: Some of the axon contacts on the relay neuron fade out. Label: removed. No retraction-then-debris sequence shown.

scenes.tts: So, which inputs lose? And what carries them away?
scenes.visual: Two question cards side by side: Which inputs lose? What carries them away?
scenes.narration: So, which inputs lose? And what carries them away?

scenes.tts: The sorting is driven partly by spontaneous waves of activity. They sweep the young retina before the eyes open.
scenes.visual: A retina with a wave of activity sweeping across it; eyelids shown closed. Label: spontaneous retinal waves.
scenes.narration: The sorting is driven partly by spontaneous waves of activity. They sweep the young retina before the eyes open.

scenes.tts: Predict. If activity biases the outcome, which inputs should lose more often: the busier ones, or the quieter ones?
scenes.visual: Question card over two axons, one flashing often (busier), one rarely (quieter).
scenes.narration: Predict. If activity biases the outcome, which inputs should lose more often: the busier ones, or the quieter ones?

scenes.tts: In this circuit, experiments that change one eye's activity point to the quieter ones. Later, an experiment that silences one eye tests whether microglia follow.
scenes.visual: Two eyes side by side, one dimmed (quieter), one bright; the dimmed eye's territory in the dLGN shrinks. Label: in this circuit; eye-level schematic, not single axons.
scenes.narration: In this circuit, experiments that change one eye's activity point to the quieter ones. Later, an experiment that silences one eye tests whether microglia follow.

scenes.tts: For the second question, the obvious suspects are microglia, the brain's resident immune cells and its main phagocytes.
scenes.visual: A green microglial cell with fine processes sits among the retinal axons in the dLGN. Label: microglia.
scenes.narration: For the second question, the obvious suspects are microglia, the brain's resident immune cells and its main phagocytes.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea to carry through. Relative activity biases which retinal inputs lose, and microglia take relatively more from the quieter eye. Complement helps them eat part of that.
scenes.visual: Guiding-idea card: Relative activity biases which retinal inputs lose, and microglia take relatively more from the quieter eye; complement helps them eat part of that.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea to carry through. Relative activity biases which retinal inputs lose, and microglia take relatively more from the quieter eye. Complement helps them eat part of that.

scenes.tts: The rule has a scope. This is the mouse visual thalamus, in the first week and a half after birth.
scenes.visual: Scope list builds. Item 1: mouse dLGN, about P3 to P10.
scenes.narration: The rule has a scope. This is the mouse visual thalamus, in the first week and a half after birth.

scenes.tts: Complement is needed for normal sorting. These studies did not show that it carries the activity information.
scenes.visual: Item 2: complement needed; not shown to carry the activity information.
scenes.narration: Complement is needed for normal sorting. These studies did not show that it carries the activity information.

scenes.tts: And part means part. Some eating goes on without complement's receptor. Astrocytes eat synapses too.
scenes.visual: Item 3: part of the eating. Small icons: a microglial cell still eating without the receptor; an astrocyte eating a synapse.
scenes.narration: And part means part. Some eating goes on without complement's receptor. Astrocytes eat synapses too.

scenes.tts: So keep the two findings side by side. How activity and complement connect is still open.
scenes.visual: Closing card: two boxes side by side, activity biases which inputs lose and what microglia take; complement helps them eat part of it. The gap between the boxes is labelled: open.
scenes.narration: So keep the two findings side by side. How activity and complement connect is still open.
